articles.title: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
articles.raw_description: We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it. A beginner's guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it. By Jerry James · Nov 22, 2026 With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle. OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience. That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI : a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware. Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too. Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times).

articles.title: Masullo on the Riemann Hypothesis
articles.raw_description: On November 20, 2026, two attempts to prove the Riemann Hypothesis appeared. One, by Levent Alpöge working with Claude, exists mainly as 17 million lines of Lean code. The other, by Alessandro Masu… Azimuth Home About Masullo on the Riemann Hypothesis On November 20, 2026, two attempts to prove the Riemann Hypothesis appeared. One, by Levent Alpöge working with Claude, exists mainly as 17 million lines of Lean code. The other, by Alessandro Masullo, is a 940-page human-written manuscript that Ravi Vakil posted on his blog: • Ravi Vakil, Hurried announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH , Math 216 blog, November 20, 2026. • Alessandro Maria Masullo, The Music of the Primes , draft, November 20, 2026. While there’s been an enormous outpouring about the drama of this situation, so far it’s hard to find good simple accounts of Masullo’s paper. Let me try to fill this gap by sketching Masullo’s proof strategy in a very simplified way, along with some problems people have noted. Since I am not an expert on number theory, all this is very tentative and I could be making serious mistakes. Please let me know if you see some! If you also want a sketch of the Alpöge / Claude attempt, check out these: • Michael Rubinstein, The Alpöge-Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis explained for the Riemann zeta function . • Jimmie Adriazola, An end-to-end reconstruction of the Alpöge–Claude route to the Riemann hypothesis .
